faq.q: When is the best time to ride motorcycle routes in Scotland?
faq.a: May and September offer the best balance of weather, daylight hours, and lighter traffic. Summer (June-August) has better weather odds but expect more tourists and higher accommodation prices. Avoid winter unless experienced in adverse conditions.

faq.q: How much fuel range do I need for Scottish Highland routes?
faq.a: On remote routes like the NC500, fuel stations can be 60+ miles apart. Most modern bikes with 150+ mile range are fine, but fill up whenever you drop below half tank in remote areas and check station opening hours beforehand.

faq.q: Is the NC500 too busy for motorcycles in 2026?
faq.a: The NC500 has heavy motorhome and tourist traffic in peak summer months. Ride it in May or September for lighter traffic, or start very early in the morning during summer. The route remains world-class but requires timing to enjoy properly.

faq.q: What gear is essential for Scottish motorcycle touring?
faq.a: Quality waterproofs that work in sustained rain, heated grips or gloves, neck warmers, and layering system with storage for clothing changes. Carry paper maps as backup since mobile signal drops regularly in the Highlands.

faq.q: Are Scottish single-track roads suitable for touring motorcycles?
faq.a: Yes, but they require specific skills and etiquette. Use passing places to let faster traffic pass, reverse to the nearest passing place when meeting oncoming vehicles, and watch for livestock. They're slower but offer incredible scenery and solitude.

faq.q: Can I wild camp on a motorcycle tour in Scotland?
faq.a: Yes, Scotland's access rights allow wild camping. Choose discreet locations, leave no trace, and avoid staying in one spot multiple nights. Many riders prefer mixing wild camping with B&Bs for drying gear and proper rest after long riding days.

Motorcycle Routes Scotland: The Ultimate Guide to Riding North of the Border

I'll be straight with you—Scotland has ruined me for riding anywhere else in Britain. I've spent the last few seasons exploring every corner of this magnificent country on two wheels, and I keep coming back. The roads are quieter, the scenery is more dramatic, and there's a raw quality to the riding that you just don't get down south.

Whether you're planning your first Scottish tour or you're a seasoned rider looking for fresh tarmac, I've put together everything I've learned from countless miles in the saddle up here. This isn't just a list of roads—it's the practical stuff you actually need to know before you point your bike north.

Why Scotland is Britain's Best Motorcycle Touring Destination

Look, I love Wales. The Lake District has its moments. But Scotland operates on a different scale entirely. You've got over 790 islands, mountain passes that'll make your heart race, coastal roads where you're riding between sea and sky, and enough variety to fill a lifetime of tours.

The traffic is lighter than England—significantly so once you're past Glasgow and Edinburgh. The roads are generally well-maintained, though you need to watch for surface changes and the occasional rogue pothole after winter. And the riding culture here is brilliant. Other bikers actually wave. Cafés understand that we need somewhere to dry our gear. It feels like home.

The Classic Scottish Routes You Need to Ride

The NC500: Scotland's Answer to Route 66

Everyone talks about the North Coast 500, and for good reason. I've ridden it four times now, and each trip has been different. This 516-mile loop starting from Inverness takes you around the northern Highlands, and it's genuinely world-class riding.

The reality is that the NC500 has become victim of its own success. In summer, you'll encounter motorhomes, coaches, and traffic you wouldn't expect on these remote roads. My advice? Ride it in May or September. The weather's more unpredictable, but you'll actually enjoy the roads rather than sitting behind a campervan on single-track sections.

I've written a complete breakdown of the route with all my recommended stops and alternative diversions—check out my NC500 complete guide for the full detail.

The A82: Glen Coe and Loch Lomond

The A82 from Glasgow to Fort William is probably the most ridden motorcycle route in Scotland, and it earns that popularity. The section through Glen Coe is properly spectacular—mountains rising on both sides, the road flowing through the valley with enough bends to keep things interesting.

I won't pretend it's perfect. The surface can be patchy, especially after winter freeze-thaw cycles. There are average speed cameras through some sections. And yes, you'll encounter tourist traffic, particularly around Loch Lomond in summer.

But ride it early morning or on a clear evening, and you'll understand why this is essential Scotland. The drama of the landscape makes every other consideration worthwhile. Stop at the Green Welly Stop in Tyndrum—proper biker-friendly café with decent food and always interesting bikes in the car park.

The B Roads of Argyll and Bute

This is where Scotland gets really interesting for motorcyclists. The B-roads around Argyll—routes like the B8024 around Loch Awe, the B840 on the Cowal Peninsula, or the coastal B842 to Crinan—these are the roads that have you grinning inside your helmet.

Narrow, technical, barely any traffic, and scenery that makes you want to stop every few miles for photos. The surface quality varies more than A-roads, so keep your wits about you, but these routes reward committed riding.

I particularly love linking these together into loops. You can create multi-day tours that never touch a motorway, staying on coastal routes and mountain passes. Use the route builder tool to string together your own combinations—it's how I plan most of my Scottish trips now.

The Coastal Routes: Ayrshire to the Western Isles

The A719 and A77 down the Ayrshire coast offer brilliant sea views and flowing corners, but for me, the real magic happens when you take ferries to the islands. The routes from Ardrossan to Arran, or from Oban to Mull, open up riding that feels genuinely remote.

On Mull, the road from Craignure to Fionnphort is single-track with passing places. It's slow riding, but the landscape is incredible and you'll see more wildlife than vehicles. Skye has become busier since the bridge opened, but the roads around the north of the island—particularly up to the Old Man of Storr—are still fantastic.

For a proper adventure, consider my island to highlands route, which links island hopping with mainland mountain passes.

The A93: Cairngorms and Royal Deeside

The A93 through the Cairngorms, particularly the section from Braemar over to Glenshee, takes you to the highest public road in Britain at 670 metres. This is proper mountain riding with hairpins, elevation changes, and weather that can turn hostile without warning.

I've ridden this in July sunshine and September snow—sometimes on the same trip. The skiing infrastructure at Glenshee means there are facilities even off-season, but you need to be self-sufficient up here. Make sure you've got proper layers and waterproofs before you commit to this route.

The descent into Braemar is gorgeous, and the road east through Royal Deeside to Ballater and beyond offers gentler but no less beautiful riding through Scots pine forests and alongside the River Dee.

Practical Considerations for Scottish Touring

Weather and When to Ride

Let's address this head-on: Scottish weather is unpredictable, and you will get wet. I've had glorious sunshine in October and horizontal rain in July. The key is not trying to avoid bad weather—it's being properly equipped to ride through it.

May and September are my favourite months. Longer days than you'd think (especially in May when it barely gets dark), fewer midges, and lighter traffic. June through August offers the best weather odds but expect traffic and higher accommodation prices. October can be brilliant but days are short and many facilities close for winter.

I never ride Scotland without quality waterproofs. Not "good enough for a shower" gear—proper, tested, will-keep-you-dry-in-a-deluge kit. After too many miserable days in failed waterproofs, I invested in decent gear from SportsBikeShop, and it's transformed my Scottish tours. Being dry makes the difference between epic adventure and endurance test.

Fuel Stops and Range Management

Scotland has petrol stations, but they're not evenly distributed. On the NC500, you can go 60+ miles between fuel stops. In the Highlands, stations often close early or don't open Sundays.

I run on the rule that I fill up whenever I drop below half a tank in remote areas. Yes, it means more frequent stops, but it eliminates range anxiety. Most modern bikes will do 150+ miles on a tank, which gives you comfortable margin, but don't push it.

Useful tip: the phone apps showing petrol prices often show opening hours too. Screen-grab the locations before you lose signal.

Accommodation Strategies

Wild camping is legal in Scotland under the access rights, and I've had some brilliant nights pitched up in lay-bys or quiet spots with million-pound views. But realistically, after a full day's riding, I usually prefer a proper bed.

Book ahead in summer, especially around the NC500 and popular areas. Small hotels and B&Bs often have secure parking and are brilliant for drying gear. Bunkhouses and hostels work well for budget tours and you'll meet other riders.

I use a mix of pre-booked and spontaneous accommodation. First and last nights booked, middle section flexible depending on weather and how I'm feeling. The trip planning tool helps me identify backup options so I'm never completely stuck.

Road Conditions and Hazards

Scottish roads present specific challenges. Single-track roads with passing places require etiquette—if someone's behind you and faster, pull over and let them pass. If you're meeting oncoming traffic, whoever's closest to a passing place reverses to it.

Livestock on roads is common, especially in the Highlands and islands. Sheep are genuinely stupid and will step out without warning. Deer are more dangerous—they can total a bike. Dawn and dusk are highest risk times.

Surface quality varies dramatically. You'll go from smooth A-roads to B-roads with gravel, potholes, and patched sections. The freeze-thaw cycle destroys road surfaces here, and repairs happen slowly in remote areas. Stay alert, especially on unfamiliar roads.

Scottish touring requires a different mindset than riding in England. It's not about chasing lap times or covering maximum miles—it's about adapting to conditions, enjoying the journey, and remembering that the weather and wildlife don't care about your schedule.

Essential Kit for Scottish Routes

Beyond the obvious helmet, boots, and jacket, Scottish touring demands specific additions to your kit list. I've refined this through trial and error—mostly error, to be honest.

Heated grips or gloves make a massive difference. Even in summer, Scottish mornings can be cold, and wet hands get cold fast. Neck warmers or balaclavas that fit under your helmet are essential for mountain passes.

A tank bag or top box for layers is crucial. I start rides in full waterproofs and thermal layers, then strip down as the day warms, then add everything back on when the weather turns. You need somewhere to put this stuff.

Phone mounts and battery packs keep navigation working, but carry paper maps as backup. Signal drops regularly in the Highlands, and while GPS works without signal, it's reassuring to have analog backup.

Check my complete motorcycle touring packing checklist for the full breakdown of what I carry on Scottish tours.

Hidden Gems and Lesser-Known Routes

The Trossachs Loop

The area between Loch Lomond and Stirling offers brilliant riding that's overshadowed by the more famous routes further north. The A821 Duke's Pass from Aberfoyle to Loch Katrine is a fantastic road—technical, tree-lined, proper motorcycle territory. Link it with the A84 through Strathyre and you've got a superb day's riding from Glasgow or Edinburgh.

Galloway Forest Park

Down in southwest Scotland, the roads through Galloway Forest Park get overlooked by riders heading north. The A712 from New Galloway to Newton Stewart is called the Queen's Way and runs through stunning forest scenery with surprisingly few other vehicles.

This area also has Britain's first Dark Sky Park, so if you're camping, the night skies are incredible. The riding isn't as dramatic as the Highlands, but it's excellent practice for single-track technique and the roads are often completely empty.

The North East Coast

While everyone rides the west coast, the route from Aberdeen up to John o'Groats via the A90 and A9 offers brilliant coastal scenery and even lighter traffic. The villages between Stonehaven and Fraserburgh have proper character, and you'll find excellent fish and chips in places that never see tourist crowds.

Planning Your Scottish Motorcycle Route

I've learned that the best Scottish tours balance ambition with flexibility. A rigid itinerary covering 300 miles a day sounds great until you hit rain, wind, or find a road so good you want to ride it twice.

My approach now is to identify must-see sections and book accommodation around those, but leave entire days flexible. If the weather's brilliant, I'll ride further. If it's grim, I'll find a café with WiFi and plan the next day properly.

Think about loops rather than point-to-point routes when possible. It means you can base yourself somewhere for a couple of nights and ride different routes each day without packing and unpacking your bike constantly.

Consider the time of day too. That Instagram-famous road at 2pm on a Saturday will be busy. The same road at 7am or 8pm might be empty and the light will be better for photos anyway.

Final Thoughts: Just Go Ride Scotland

I could write another 2,000 words about Scottish motorcycle routes and still not cover everything. The Applecross Peninsula, the Road to the Isles, the Borders region, Orkney, the Hebrides—each deserves its own guide.

But here's what matters: Scotland is rideable right now, and every season you delay is a season of brilliant riding you're missing. You don't need the perfect bike, the perfect weather window, or weeks of free time. A long weekend is enough to scratch the surface.

Start with a manageable loop—maybe Glasgow to Fort William via Glen Coe, across to the west coast, and back via Loch Lomond. Or Edinburgh to the Borders and back. Build confidence, test your gear, learn what kind of Scottish riding you enjoy most.

Then plan the bigger trip. The NC500, a island-hopping tour, or a complete circuit of Scotland. Use what you learned on the shorter trip to plan better. The roads will still be there, and they'll be just as good.

Scotland has made me a better rider. The conditions demand attention, the distances teach patience, and the scenery reminds you why we do this in the first place. I'll see you up there—I'll be the one grinning despite the rain.
